newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM threatens opponents after poll win.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM threatens opponents after poll win.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Sunday seized on a spectacular by-election victory to threaten parliamentary opponents into backing his economic reforms.
The Liberal-National government won the by-election despite almost every factor favouring the Labor opposition.

Most ominously for the Labor opposition, the government candidate was returned with an increased majority, which Howard interpreted as confirming voters' satisfaction with the government they elected in March and its policies.
"I think one of the messages coming out of yesterday loudly and clearly is 'We didn't make a mistake, we wanted a change'," Howard said in a speech to a Liberal Party conference.
"And for those who would endeavour unreasonably to frustrate that change: 'Get out of the way and let the new crowd have a fair go'."

The strength of the win will come as a morale booster to Howard's Liberals after a turbulent week in which two junior ministers were forced to resign because their share holdings breached government guidelines.
Almost all of the government's economic reforms face some degree of resistance from other parties, who together can control the upper house of parliament, the Senate.
To reform the industrial relations system, for example, the government is trying to woo the Australian Democrats, a minor party that is demanding changes to secure its votes.

The by-election was held in a traditionally safe working class Labor seat that fell to the Liberal Party in one of the more astonishing results from the March election, a landslide that ended 13 years of Labor power.
Since by-elections usually attract strong protest votes against the government of the day, Labor had hoped the weekend would see the return of its traditional supporters.

Instead there was a further swing to the government, which was all the more surprising because of the government's economic reforms, which include a tough budget and an unpopular plan to partly privatise telecoms carrier Telstra Corp Ltd.

Election officials said on Saturday night that, with 80 percent of the vote counted, Liberal candidate Jackie Kelly beat former Labor Party minister Ross Free with more than 56.34 percent of votes after sharing out second-preference votes in Sydney's Lindsay constituency.
The result represented a swing to the Liberals of almost five percent on top of an 11.4 percent swing Kelly achieved in the March general election.
Opposition leader Kim Beazley told Labor supporters Howard's administration was new and therefore still popular.
"It's a government still in its honeymoon period," he told a Labor Party conference in Adelaide on Sunday.
"After 13 years of us in office they are not going to change their minds anytime soon."
Howard warned his party not to relax. "We must guard against complacency," he said.
Government sources said the by-election might embolden the government into pursuing braver economic reforms.
"It certainly strengthens the hand of those pushing for more courageous policies," said one senior official.
The by-election was held because the High Court declared ineligible the Liberal candidate who won the seat in March, following a court challenge by Labor.
Kelly held New Zealand citizenship and had a government job at the time of the election, disqualifying her. She quit the job, changed her citizenship and stood for the seat again.
